why_how.text: The vehicle you bring is part of the road test, so a missing document or a broken window can stop the test before it starts.

scenario.text: Alex brings a newer car to the road test with its registration and insurance card.

reasoning.text: The car's seat belts must be fastened and adjusted, and its parking assistance must stay off.

result.text: Alex parks by hand, with every maneuver done without driver assistance.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking driver assistance features are fine to use on the road test because the car came with them.

correction.text: Advanced Driver Assistance Systems such as auto-drive and parking assistance are banned, so every maneuver is done by hand.

prompt.text: Can a road test applicant let the car's parking assistance handle parallel parking?

answer.text: No, driver assistance systems are banned during the test.

rationale.text: Every maneuver on the road test must be done by hand.

narration.text: This lesson finishes the list of rules for the vehicle you bring to the road test. You already know it needs working brakes, lights, signals, horn, mirrors and tires. Here are the next items. For the road test, the driver and passenger side windows must work and both front doors must open and close properly. Then we will add the paperwork you must carry for the vehicle, the seat belt rule tied to model year, and one rule about modern driver assistance features that surprises many applicants. Each item on the list is its own requirement, so keep a mental checklist as you prepare.

The vehicle needs papers as well as working parts. At the road test you must show proof of current registration and current automobile liability insurance for the vehicle. Notice the word current in both items. An expired registration or an old insurance card does not meet the rule. The proof also has to be for the vehicle you are testing in, so if you borrow a car, make sure its own registration and insurance proof come along with it. In short, registration and liability insurance are the two documents, and both must be current for the car you drive on the test.

A road test vehicle that is a nineteen seventy-two model or newer must have seat belts, and they must be fastened and adjusted properly. The rule is tied to the age of the car. The seat belt requirement for a road test vehicle depends on model year, applying to nineteen seventy-two and newer vehicles. So for almost any car you are likely to bring, plan on belts being worn correctly from the start of the test to the end. If your car is older than that, this seat belt rule for the road test does not cover it, but every other item on the list still does.

lines.text: Every maneuver is done by hand.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many newer cars can park themselves or help steer, and it is tempting to let them work during the test. Advanced Driver Assistance Systems such as auto-drive and parking assistance are banned during the road test, so every maneuver must be done by hand. The examiner is grading your driving, so the features that would do part of the job for you are not allowed. Plan to turn them off and handle every move yourself, including parking. Auto-drive and parking assistance are the two examples the manual names, and the ban covers driver assistance systems in general.

Here is a quick check: your car has a parking assistance feature. During the road test, may you let it handle parallel parking? Decide before the answer. No. Advanced Driver Assistance Systems such as auto-drive and parking assistance are banned during the road test, so every maneuver must be done by hand. If you were unsure, remember that the ban names parking assistance directly, alongside auto-drive, so there is no gray area for parking. The same ban covers auto-drive, so the whole test, from pulling away to parking, is driven by you.

To close, a road test vehicle needs working driver and passenger side windows and front doors that open and close properly. You must show current registration and current liability insurance for that vehicle. A nineteen seventy-two or newer model must have seat belts that are fastened and adjusted properly. Driver assistance systems such as auto-drive and parking assistance are banned, so every maneuver is yours. Put these together with the equipment list from the earlier lesson and your vehicle will be ready. Keep this checklist close as you prepare.

why_how.text: Every vehicle driven in Arizona needs the right kind of insurance, and the minimum amounts appear often in practice questions.
Keeping proof in the car matters because officers ask for it at traffic stops and crashes.

scenario.text: Jordan buys a policy from an insurer licensed in Arizona for a car mainly driven in Phoenix.

reasoning.text: The policy is Arizona-based and meets the minimum amounts for bodily injury and property damage.

result.text: Jordan checks that the insurer's VIN matches the registration and keeps proof in the glove box.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking any insurance policy from any company satisfies Arizona's rule.

correction.text: The policy must come from an insurer licensed in Arizona and be Arizona-based for where the vehicle is mostly driven.

memory_support.text: Licensed insurer, Arizona policy, right VIN, proof aboard.

prompt.text: What is Arizona's minimum bodily injury coverage when two or more people are hurt?

rationale.text: The minimums are twenty-five thousand dollars for one person, fifty thousand for two or more, and fifteen thousand for property damage.

narration.text: This lesson covers the insurance rules for every motor vehicle on Arizona roads. Start with the basic requirement. Every motor vehicle driven on Arizona roads must be covered by a liability insurance policy from a company licensed to do business in Arizona. From there we will add where the policy must be based, the three minimum dollar amounts, how to check the VIN your insurer reports, and why proof of insurance has to ride along with you every time you drive. Each of these rules applies to every vehicle you drive, not only to the car you take to the road test.

lines.text: Matches where the car is driven.

narration.text: The basic rule has a second part. The policy must be an Arizona-based policy that matches where the vehicle is mainly driven. The manual puts the two parts together in one reminder. Having a policy is only half the rule: the policy must come from an insurer licensed in Arizona and be an Arizona-based policy for where the vehicle is mostly driven. So check both the company and the policy when you buy insurance, especially if you are moving from another state with an old policy. A policy that meets only one of the two parts does not meet the rule.

lines.text: Bodily injury, two or more people.

narration.text: Arizona's minimum liability coverage for a private passenger vehicle is twenty-five thousand dollars for bodily injury to one person, fifty thousand dollars for bodily injury to two or more people, and fifteen thousand dollars for property damage. The two bodily injury minimums differ by headcount, while property damage has its own lower minimum. Picture three boxes: one injured person, two or more injured people, and damaged property, each with its own amount. The pattern to remember is that the amounts rise from property, to one person, to two or more people.

Here is the trap. Because the numbers look alike, people swap them, or think property damage carries the largest minimum. It is the reverse. Property damage has the lowest of the three minimums at fifteen thousand dollars, one injured person is twenty-five thousand dollars, and two or more injured people is fifty thousand dollars. When an answer choice puts twenty-five thousand dollars next to property damage, it has mixed up the boxes. Keep the pairs in order: property damage at fifteen thousand dollars, one person at twenty-five thousand, and two or more people at fifty thousand.

title.text: VIN and proof in the car

lines.text: Ask for a resubmission if not.

narration.text: Two habits keep your insurance working for you. Check that the VIN your insurance company reports matches the VIN on your registration, and ask the insurer to resubmit the correct VIN if it does not. You must keep proof of current insurance in the vehicle whenever you drive, because officers ask for it at traffic stops and at crashes. A correct VIN and proof in the glove box take only minutes to check, and they protect you at a stop or after a crash. Officers can ask for that proof at a traffic stop or after a crash, so it belongs in the car on every trip.

lines.text: Two or more people are hurt.
What is the bodily injury minimum?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: in a crash, two or more people are injured. What is Arizona's minimum bodily injury coverage for that case? Decide before you hear the answer. It is fifty thousand dollars. For a single injured person the minimum is twenty-five thousand dollars, and property damage has its own lower minimum of fifteen thousand dollars. If you said twenty-five thousand, you answered the one-person case instead of the two-or-more case. Matching the number of injured people to the right amount is the whole skill this question tests.

To sum up, every motor vehicle on Arizona roads needs liability insurance from a company licensed to do business in Arizona, on an Arizona-based policy that matches where the vehicle is mainly driven. The minimums are twenty-five thousand dollars for one injured person, fifty thousand for two or more, and fifteen thousand for property damage. Make sure the VIN your insurer reports matches your registration, and keep proof of current insurance in the vehicle every time you drive. Together these rules cover every vehicle driven on Arizona roads.

why_how.text: MVD learns about insurance changes directly from insurers, so a lapse can quickly put your registration and license at risk.
The National Driver Register check means problems in another state can follow you to Arizona.

scenario.text: Taylor's insurer reports that Taylor's policy is no longer active.

reasoning.text: MVD sends Taylor an inquiry, and without proper insurance and a correct VIN, MVD may suspend the registration, the license or both.

result.text: Taylor checks the Manage Insurance option online to see what MVD has on file.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a lapse in insurance can only cost you the vehicle registration.

correction.text: It can suspend the driver license as well, not just the registration.

prompt.text: What can MVD suspend if your insurance lapses?

answer.text: Your vehicle registration, your driver license, or both.

rationale.text: Not keeping proper Arizona insurance with a correct VIN can lead to suspension of the registration, the license, or both.

narration.text: This lesson explains how MVD keeps track of insurance and of problem drivers. Start with the reporting flow. Insurance companies report every new policy, cancellation and non-renewal to MVD, and MVD sends you an inquiry if your insurer says your policy is no longer active. Then we will look at what a lapse can cost you, a quick way to check your own record, the National Driver Register that every application is checked against, and what false information on an application can lead to. Each of these links back to the insurance rules from the last lesson.

Here is the penalty the manual describes. Not keeping proper Arizona insurance with a correct VIN on file can lead MVD to suspend your vehicle registration, your driver license, or both. Notice that the rule is about two things at once: keeping proper Arizona insurance, and having the correct VIN on file. Either problem can start the process. The easiest protection is the check you learned earlier, comparing the VIN your insurer reports with the VIN on your registration. So a wrong VIN on file can lead to the same suspension as a missing policy.

lines.text: A lapse can reach the license.

narration.text: Here is the trap. People assume insurance is about the car, so a lapse can only touch the car's registration. The manual says otherwise. Losing proper insurance or carrying a wrong VIN can suspend the vehicle registration and the driver license, not just the registration. To see what MVD has on file, use the tool it names. You can confirm the insurance MVD has on file by using the Manage Insurance option at AZMVDNow.gov. In other words, the same lapse can affect both the vehicle and your own driver license, which is why checking the insurance MVD has on file is useful.

lines.text: A nationwide system on problem drivers.

narration.text: Arizona is connected to a national system. Arizona belongs to the National Driver Register, a nationwide computer system about problem drivers, and every Arizona license application is checked against it. Here is what happens when it finds something. If the register shows outstanding or unresolved actions against you in another state, Arizona will not issue you a license. So unresolved trouble in another state does not stay behind when you move. The check happens on every Arizona license application, not only on some of them.

lines.text: Register problems block a new license.

narration.text: Two rules here end in different places. First, false statements. Giving false information on your application can get your Arizona license canceled. Second, the comparison the manual draws between the register and false statements. The National Driver Register can block an Arizona license because of unresolved actions in another state, while false statements on the application lead to cancellation of a license already issued. So the register stops a license from being issued, while false information can take away a license you already hold.

Here is a quick check: your insurance lapsed and was never replaced. What can MVD suspend? The answer is your vehicle registration, your driver license, or both. Not keeping proper Arizona insurance with a correct VIN on file can lead MVD to suspend your vehicle registration, your driver license, or both. If you answered only the registration, look again at the manual's own reminder. Losing proper insurance or carrying a wrong VIN can suspend the vehicle registration and the driver license, not just the registration. Insurance problems reach the driver as well as the car.

lines.text: Lapses can suspend registration and license.

narration.text: To finish, insurers report every new policy, cancellation and non-renewal to MVD, which sends you an inquiry when a policy is reported inactive. Without proper Arizona insurance and a correct VIN on file, MVD can suspend your registration, your license, or both, and you can check your file with the Manage Insurance option online. Every license application is checked against the National Driver Register, unresolved actions in another state block an Arizona license, and false information on an application can get a license canceled.

why_how.text: Once you become a resident, Arizona expects you to get its license and registration right away.
The exceptions for students and seasonal farm work keep some people from being counted as residents.

scenario.text: Casey moves to Tucson for a new office job and enrolls two children in school at the resident rate.

reasoning.text: Working in Arizona and enrolling children without paying non-resident tuition are both residency conditions.

result.text: Casey must get an Arizona license and vehicle registration right away.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the seven months must be spent in Arizona in a row.

correction.text: Residency by time is seven months in total within a calendar year, wherever your permanent home is.

memory_support.text: Any one condition, act right away.

prompt.text: A visitor spends four months early in the year and three months later in the same year in Arizona. Is the visitor a resident for licensing?

answer.text: Yes, because the months add up to seven in that calendar year.

rationale.text: The seven months are counted in total within the calendar year, not in a row.

narration.text: This lesson explains when Arizona treats you as a resident for licensing. Here is the core rule. State law requires you to get an Arizona driver license and vehicle registration right away once any one of the listed residency conditions applies to you. The rest of the lesson goes through the conditions one by one: work and school, business vehicles, licenses and tuition, time spent in the state, and voter registration. Then we cover the two groups the manual carves out, seasonal farm workers and out-of-state students.

The first conditions involve daily life. Those conditions include working in Arizona (seasonal farm work excepted) and enrolling children in school without paying the non-resident tuition rate. They also include having a business office in Arizona that bases and operates vehicles here, or running a business that moves goods or passengers within Arizona. Each of these on its own is enough to start the duty to get an Arizona license and registration. Remember that seasonal farm work is the one kind of job the manual leaves out, which we will come back to shortly.

More conditions come from official choices you make. Getting a state license or paying school tuition at the resident rate also makes you a resident for licensing purposes. Being registered to vote in Arizona is another condition that triggers the duty to get an Arizona license. Notice how these connect to other parts of this section: registering to vote is optional, but if you do register, it also means you must get an Arizona license. Each of these, like the others in this lesson, is enough on its own to create the duty to get an Arizona license right away.

lines.text: Seven months or more in total.

narration.text: The time rule works even for people who keep a home elsewhere. Staying in Arizona for seven months or more in total during any calendar year makes you a resident no matter where your permanent home is. The counting method matters too. Residency by time is seven months in total within a calendar year, counted regardless of where your permanent home is, not seven consecutive months. So add up every stretch you spend in the state during the calendar year. A winter visitor who spends seven months here in total during a calendar year is counted as a resident for licensing.

lines.text: Seasonal farm work does not count.

narration.text: Here is where people trip up. Working in Arizona usually makes you a resident, but there is one kind of job that does not. Seasonal agricultural work is the one kind of Arizona job that does not trigger residency. Students are the other exception, and it holds even when they work. An out-of-state student taking seven or more semester hours is not considered an Arizona resident, even with a job in the state. Out-of-state students with seven or more semester hours stay non-residents even if employed, which overrides the general rule that working in Arizona makes you a resident.

Here is a quick check: a visitor spends four months in Arizona early in the year and three more months later in the same calendar year. Is the visitor a resident for licensing? Yes. Residency by time is seven months in total within a calendar year, counted regardless of where your permanent home is, not seven consecutive months. The months do not have to be consecutive, and the visitor's permanent home elsewhere does not change the result. That is the detail this check is designed to catch. Total time in the calendar year is what counts.

lines.text: Any condition means a license right away.
Seven months total in a year.
Farm work and students are excepted.

narration.text: To sum up, once any listed residency condition applies, state law requires an Arizona license and registration right away. Conditions include working here, enrolling children at the resident rate, basing business vehicles here or moving goods or passengers within Arizona, getting a state license, paying resident tuition, registering to vote, and spending seven months or more in total in a calendar year. Seasonal agricultural work does not count, and out-of-state students taking seven or more semester hours stay non-residents even with a job.

why_how.text: The license application doubles as a voter registration form, so it helps to know what is optional and what is required.
Missing the registration deadline or forgetting to re-register after a move can keep you from voting.

scenario.text: Morgan is seventeen but will turn eighteen before the next General Election.

reasoning.text: Morgan is a United States citizen and an Arizona resident with no disqualifying conviction.

result.text: Morgan can register on the license application, and must be registered twenty-nine days before an election to vote in it.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you must already be eighteen on the day you register.

correction.text: The age test is measured on the next General Election date, so turning eighteen by then is enough.

memory_support.text: Eighteen by election day, registered twenty-nine days ahead.

prompt.text: You moved to a new address last month. What must you do to keep voting?

rationale.text: When you change your address you must register again, and you must be registered twenty-nine days before an election.

narration.text: This lesson covers the voter registration portion of the license and ID application. Start with the basic choice. The driver license or ID application includes a voter registration portion you can fill out at the same time, but registering is not required to get a license. Then we will cover how your choice is protected, the penalty for a false registration, who may register, other ways to register, and the timing rules you need to vote in a coming election. None of these voter rules is required to get a license, but each one matters if you choose to register.

lines.text: A registration is used only for voting.

narration.text: Your choice is protected either way. If you decline to register to vote, that choice stays confidential, and if you do register, the application is kept confidential and used only for voter registration. The flip side is that lying on a registration is a serious crime. Submitting a false voter registration is a Class six felony in Arizona. So the form is easy and private to use, but it must be filled out truthfully. Keep both ideas together: the system protects your privacy, and the information you give must be true, because a false registration is a felony under Arizona law.

lines.text: Eighteen by the next General Election.

narration.text: Here are the eligibility rules. To register to vote you must be at least eighteen by the next General Election, a United States citizen and an Arizona resident. You also cannot have a felony conviction unless your civil rights were restored, and you cannot have been adjudicated incompetent. Read the restored rights part carefully: a felony conviction blocks registration only when civil rights have not been restored. Being adjudicated incompetent also prevents registration, so there are two separate barriers on top of the age, citizenship and residency rules.

lines.text: Age is checked at the next election.

narration.text: Here is the trap. People think a seventeen year old must wait until their birthday to register. The manual measures age on a different date. The voter age test is measured on the next General Election date, so an applicant who will be eighteen on or before that date can register. So a seventeen year old who will turn eighteen on or before the next General Election can already register, as long as the other rules are met. The age, citizenship and residency rules all still apply, so the election date only changes how the age part is measured.

The license application is not the only route. Besides the license application, you can register to vote online at AZMVDNow.gov or on a separate form available at MVD offices. There is also a deadline and a price to know. To vote in an upcoming election you must be registered twenty-nine days before it, and registering costs nothing. So you can register any of several ways at no cost, but it has to be done well before the election. Online registration at the portal and the separate form at MVD offices are both available in addition to the voter section on the application.

Two timing rules are easy to blend together. When you change your address you must register to vote again. The manual puts them side by side. You must be registered twenty-nine days before an election to vote in it, and moving to a new address means you must register to vote again. One rule is about how far ahead you must register, and the other is about what a move does to your registration. Twenty-nine days is the registration deadline before an election, and a change of address means registering again, so a move close to an election deserves extra attention.

lines.text: What happens to your voter registration?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you moved to a new address last month. What must you do to keep voting? The answer is to register to vote again. When you change your address you must register to vote again. And remember the deadline that goes with it. To vote in an upcoming election you must be registered twenty-nine days before it, and registering costs nothing. If you thought your registration follows you automatically, this is the rule to remember. Registering again costs nothing, just like registering the first time, and it can be done the same ways.

lines.text: Eighteen by the next General Election.

narration.text: To close, the voter portion of the application is optional, your choice stays confidential, and a false registration is a Class six felony. You may register if you will be at least eighteen by the next General Election, are a United States citizen and an Arizona resident, and have no unrestored felony conviction or adjudication of incompetence. You can also register online or on a separate MVD form. Be registered twenty-nine days before an election, registering is free, and a change of address means registering again.

title.text: Donor, medical code and Social Security

why_how.text: The application lets you make two personal choices, organ donation and a medical indicator, alongside one requirement you cannot skip.

scenario.text: Riley wants a medical condition indicator on the license and also wants to be an organ donor.

reasoning.text: Riley brings a statement signed by a licensed physician and checks the Donate Life AZ box.

result.text: Riley still must provide proof of a valid Social Security number, as every applicant does.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the medical indicator is required for anyone with a health condition.

correction.text: The medical indicator is optional and requested with documentation; the Social Security proof is the mandatory part.

memory_support.text: Donor and medical: your choice; Social Security: required.

prompt.text: Which item on the license application is required rather than optional?

answer.text: Proof of a valid Social Security number.

rationale.text: State and federal law require Social Security proof, while the medical indicator and donor box are optional.

narration.text: This lesson covers the last items on the license and ID application. Start with a personal choice. The license or ID application has a box to join the Donate Life AZ Registry as an organ and tissue donor. Then we will look at the other ways to sign up as a donor, the medical condition indicator and the paperwork it needs, and the one item in this lesson that is required rather than optional: proof of your Social Security number. Two of these are choices you make, and the last one is required by state and federal law, so we will treat them differently.

If you miss the box on the paper application, there are other routes. You can also sign up as a donor by saying yes at an MVD or third-party office, by checking the box when applying online at AZMVDNow.gov, or through DonateLifeAZ.org. Every one of these routes leads to the same registry, so pick whichever fits your visit. Signing up is a choice, and the manual presents it as an option on the application rather than a requirement. The options are saying yes at an MVD or third-party office, checking the box online at the portal, or going through DonateLifeAZ.org.

lines.text: Space on the license for a condition.

narration.text: Your license can carry a medical note. Your license has space for a medical condition indicator for conditions that may need immediate attention. Getting it takes documents. Getting the medical code takes paperwork about the condition: a statement signed by a licensed physician or by a registered nurse practitioner, or an advanced healthcare directive. So the indicator is something you ask for and support with paperwork, not something MVD adds by itself. The paperwork can be a statement from a licensed physician or a registered nurse practitioner, or an advanced healthcare directive.

Here is the trap. Because the medical indicator appears on the same application as required items, some people think it is mandatory. It is not. The medical condition indicator is an optional entry you request with documentation, whereas proof of a valid Social Security number is mandatory under state and federal law. The requirement in this part of the application is the Social Security proof. State and federal law require you to provide proof of a valid Social Security number when you apply. Every applicant must provide it.

Here is a quick check: of the donor box, the medical indicator and proof of a Social Security number, which one is required? The answer is proof of a valid Social Security number. State and federal law require you to provide proof of a valid Social Security number when you apply. The other two are choices you make, and the medical one needs supporting paperwork. The medical condition indicator is an optional entry you request with documentation, whereas proof of a valid Social Security number is mandatory under state and federal law.

To finish, the license or ID application has a box to join the Donate Life AZ Registry, and you can also sign up by saying yes at an office, checking the box online or using DonateLifeAZ.org. A medical condition indicator is available for conditions that may need immediate attention, with a statement from a licensed physician or registered nurse practitioner, or an advanced healthcare directive. Proof of a valid Social Security number is required by state and federal law. Choose the options you want, and bring the required proof.
